title: Architecture: MVVM, Clean, TCA & Modularization
scopeHtml: Scope: MVVM with @Observable, repository pattern, Clean Architecture, unidirectional flow, The Composable Architecture, feature modules.

notes.title: Baseline and the architecture landscape
notes.html:
Baseline for this track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 as the minimum target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials. We use @Observable, SwiftData, async/await, actors and Swift Testing. Legacy forms (ObservableObject, Combine, XCTest, completion handlers) are labelled "old codebases". Anything new or fast-moving is marked verify.

Android equivalent first. In Android the official guidance is MVVM (or MVI) with a ViewModel, a repository, optional use cases, Hilt, and Gradle modules. In iOS the landscape is more fragmented: Apple's own MVC (UIKit), MVVM (most SwiftUI apps), VIPER/Clean (large legacy codebases), and unidirectional frameworks such as The Composable Architecture (TCA).

Android iOS
ViewModel + StateFlow @Observable class (or TCA Store)
Repository Repository protocol + concrete type
Use case / interactor Use case struct or function (optional)
Hilt / Koin Constructor injection, @Environment, Factory, swift-dependencies
Gradle feature modules Swift Package Manager local packages / targets
sealed interface UiState enum with associated values
MVI / Redux (Orbit, MVIKotlin) TCA, ReSwift (older)

The honest summary. There is no single iOS standard like Google's guide to app architecture. Teams choose by size, testability needs and how much they trust third-party frameworks. Interviewers want you to defend a choice, not recite one.

Real industry examples. Airbnb publicly moved toward a unidirectional approach on iOS; Uber built RIBs (router, interactor, builder) for huge scale; Point-Free's TCA is used by many mid-size apps; most startups ship plain MVVM with @Observable.

Analogy. Architectures are building codes: a garden shed needs none, a skyscraper needs strict ones. Choose by the size of the building.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "MVVM is the iOS standard". Apple never mandated it; SwiftUI itself reduces the need for a separate view model in small cases.
  • Saying Clean Architecture is required for testability. Protocol-based seams are enough.
  • Mixing up the Android ViewModel lifecycle with an iOS view model (next section).

notes.title: MVVM with @Observable
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android a ViewModel is owned by a ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity, Fragment, NavBackStackEntry), survives configuration change, exposes StateFlow, and is cleared by the framework. In iOS a view model is a plain Swift class. There is no lifecycle owner and no ViewModelStore. The view owns it, usually through @State, and it lives exactly as long as the view's identity lives.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@Observable
@MainActor
final class ProductListViewModel {
    private(set) var state: LoadState<[Product]> = .idle
    var query = ""

    private let repository: ProductRepository

    init(repository: ProductRepository) {
        self.repository = repository
    }

    func load() async {
        state = .loading
        do {
            state = .content(try await repository.products(matching: query))
        } catch {
            state = .failed(error.localizedDescription)
        }
    }
}

struct ProductListView: View {
    @State private var viewModel: ProductListViewModel

    init(repository: ProductRepository) {
        _viewModel = State(initialValue: ProductListViewModel(repository: repository))
    }

    var body: some View {
        content
            .task { await viewModel.load() }          // cancelled automatically when the view disappears
            .searchable(text: $viewModel.query)
    }
    @ViewBuilder private var content: some View { /* switch on state */ }
}
@HiltViewModel
class ProductListViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repository: ProductRepository
) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<LoadState<List<Product>>>(LoadState.Idle)
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun load(query: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.value = LoadState.Loading
        _state.value = try { LoadState.Content(repository.products(query)) }
                       catch (e: Exception) { LoadState.Failed(e.message) }
    }
}

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(vm: ProductListViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.load("") }
}

What @Observable gives you. The macro (Observation framework, iOS 17+) rewrites stored properties so that reads inside body register a dependency and writes notify only the views that read that property. No @Published, no objectWillChange. Mark the class @MainActor so state mutations are checked by the compiler under Swift 6 strict concurrency.

Ownership rules (the source of many bugs).

  • @State private var vm = VM(): the view creates and owns it. SwiftUI keeps the instance alive across body re-evaluations, tied to the view's identity in the tree.
  • A plain let vm: VM or @Bindable var vm: VM: someone else owns it; this view only reads.
  • Passing it through @Environment for app-wide objects.
  • With @State and an init, the default value expression is evaluated on every init of the view struct, but only the first instance is kept. Heavy work in the view model's init is therefore wasted repeatedly. Keep init cheap and start work in .task.

Lifecycle differences vs Android.

  • No onCleared(). Cleanup happens through deinit of the class (ARC) and through structured concurrency: a .task is cancelled when the view leaves the hierarchy.
  • No survive-rotation concept: the view is not destroyed on rotation, so state is not lost.
  • Process death restoration is your job (@SceneStorage, persisted data). There is no SavedStateHandle.
  • A ViewModel shared between screens in Android via a nav graph scope has no direct equivalent; share a model object through the parent view or the environment.

Unit testing the view model needs no framework tricks:

import Testing

@MainActor
struct ProductListViewModelTests {
    @Test func loadSetsContent() async {
        let repo = FakeProductRepository(result: .success([.sample]))
        let vm = ProductListViewModel(repository: repo)
        await vm.load()
        #expect(vm.state == .content([.sample]))
    }
}

Legacy form (old codebases). ObservableObject with @Published properties, @StateObject for ownership, @ObservedObject for borrowed references, and Combine pipelines (sink, assign, store(in: &cancellables)). Every @Published change invalidated every view observing the object. Moving to @Observable reduces over-invalidation but changes ownership semantics, so migrate feature by feature.

Real examples. Apple's own sample apps (Fruta, Food Truck) moved to @Observable models. Startups using Firebase and SwiftData often skip the view model for simple screens, using @Query directly in the view.

Analogy. An Android ViewModel is a hotel guest managed by the hotel (the framework). An iOS view model is a houseplant that sits in your own room: it lives as long as you keep the room.

Common interview traps.

  • Using @State for a model passed in from outside; the passed instance is ignored after the first init.
  • Forgetting @MainActor and then mutating UI state from a background task.
  • Expecting .task to survive navigation: it is cancelled when the view disappears, so the in-flight request dies.
  • Creating the view model inside body, which recreates it on every re-render.

notes.title: State modelling with enums
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin you model screen state with a sealed interface UiState (Loading, Content, Error) or a single data class with flags. In Swift an enum with associated values is the same tool, and switch is exhaustive, so the compiler forces you to handle every case.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum LoadState<Value: Equatable>: Equatable {
    case idle
    case loading
    case content(Value)
    case failed(String)
}

struct ProductListView: View {
    let state: LoadState<[Product]>
    let retry: () -> Void

    var body: some View {
        switch state {
        case .idle, .loading:
            ProgressView()
        case .content(let products) where products.isEmpty:
            ContentUnavailableView("No products", systemImage: "bag")
        case .content(let products):
            List(products) { ProductRow(product: $0) }
        case .failed(let message):
            ContentUnavailableView {
                Label("Something went wrong", systemImage: "wifi.slash")
            } description: { Text(message) } actions: {
                Button("Retry", action: retry)
            }
        }
    }
}
sealed interface LoadState<out T> {
    data object Idle : LoadState<Nothing>
    data object Loading : LoadState<Nothing>
    data class Content<T>(val value: T) : LoadState<T>
    data class Failed(val message: String) : LoadState<Nothing>
}

@Composable
fun ProductListView(state: LoadState<List<Product>>, retry: () -> Unit) {
    when (state) {
        LoadState.Idle, LoadState.Loading -> CircularProgressIndicator()
        is LoadState.Content -> if (state.value.isEmpty()) EmptyView() else LazyColumn { /* ... */ }
        is LoadState.Failed -> ErrorView(state.message, retry)
    }
}

Why not booleans. isLoading, error: Error? and items: [Product] can express impossible combinations (loading with an error and items). An enum makes illegal states unrepresentable. It also makes snapshot tests trivial: one state in, one picture out.

Refinements.

  • Keep stale content during refresh: case content(Value, isRefreshing: Bool) or a separate isRefreshing flag, so a pull-to-refresh does not blank the screen.
  • Use a domain AppError enum, not String, if the UI needs to react differently (offline vs unauthorised). Typed throws exist in Swift 6 but most apps still use untyped throws plus mapping at the repository edge.
  • ContentUnavailableView (iOS 17+) is the system empty/error view; it also has .search.
  • Mark Value as Equatable only when you need to test or diff; otherwise drop the constraint.

Real examples. Apple's sample code, Point-Free's open-source projects and most Airbnb-style screens use an enum or a view-state struct. Large apps often keep a ViewState struct holding derived display strings so the view does no formatting.

Analogy. A traffic light: exactly one colour at a time, never red and green together.

Common interview traps.

  • Modelling loading and error as independent booleans.
  • Adding an @unknown default where the enum is your own (it is only needed for non-frozen external enums).
  • Putting View types or images in the state; state should be plain data.

notes.title: Repository and use-case layers
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android the repository hides data sources (Retrofit, Room, DataStore) behind a clean API and exposes Flow. In iOS the pattern is identical, except the abstraction is a protocol and results are async throws functions or AsyncStream.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
protocol ProductRepository: Sendable {
    func products(matching query: String) async throws -> [Product]
    func product(id: Int) async throws -> Product
    func updates() -> AsyncStream<[Product]>
}

struct DefaultProductRepository: ProductRepository {
    let api: ProductAPI           // network
    let cache: ProductCache       // actor or SwiftData-backed store

    func products(matching query: String) async throws -> [Product] {
        if let cached = await cache.products(for: query) { return cached }
        let dtos = try await api.search(query)
        let models = dtos.map(Product.init(dto:))     // map DTO -> domain model at the boundary
        await cache.store(models, for: query)
        return models
    }
    // ...
}
interface ProductRepository {
    suspend fun products(query: String): List<Product>
    suspend fun product(id: Int): Product
    fun updates(): Flow<List<Product>>
}

class DefaultProductRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val api: ProductApi,
    private val cache: ProductCache
) : ProductRepository {
    override suspend fun products(query: String): List<Product> {
        cache.get(query)?.let { return it }
        return api.search(query).map(Product::from).also { cache.put(query, it) }
    }
}

Layers and what each owns.

View (SwiftUI)            renders state, sends intents
  |
ViewModel (@Observable)   screen state, calls use cases / repositories
  |
Use case (optional)       one business rule, combines repositories
  |
Repository (protocol)     single source of truth for one kind of data
  |            |
Remote (URLSession)   Local (SwiftData / SQLite / files)

Use cases. Add them only when logic is shared between view models or is non-trivial. A one-line pass-through use case is noise (the same argument applies in Android). In Swift a use case can be a struct with callAsFunction, or just a function type:

struct GetFeedUseCase {
    let posts: PostRepository
    let blocklist: BlocklistRepository

    func callAsFunction() async throws -> [Post] {
        async let all = posts.feed()
        async let blocked = blocklist.blockedIDs()
        let (feed, ids) = try await (all, blocked)
        return feed.filter { !ids.contains($0.authorID) }   // structured concurrency, runs both in parallel
    }
}

Concurrency concerns (Swift 6). Repositories are used from the main actor and background tasks, so make them Sendable: structs of Sendable values, actors for mutable caches, and final class only with immutable state or internal locking. A mutable cache as a plain class fails strict concurrency checks. Use an actor for in-memory caches:

actor ProductCache {
    private var storage: [String: [Product]] = [:]
    func products(for key: String) -> [Product]? { storage[key] }
    func store(_ items: [Product], for key: String) { storage[key] = items }
}

DTO vs domain model. Decode network JSON into DTOs (Codable structs matching the server), then map to domain models used by the UI. This is the same split as Retrofit models vs domain classes. SwiftData @Model classes are not Sendable; keep them inside a ModelActor or map to value types before crossing actor boundaries.

Real examples. Airbnb, Spotify and Instagram keep a networking client layer with endpoint definitions, a repository-like service layer, and view models above. Open-source Alamofire or plain URLSession sit at the bottom; Apollo iOS is used where GraphQL is the backend.

Analogy. A repository is a librarian: you ask for a book, and you never need to know whether it came from the shelf (cache) or from another library (network).

Common interview traps.

  • Returning DTOs or SwiftData models straight to the UI, leaking storage details everywhere.
  • Making a repository a singleton with mutable global state, which blocks testing and breaks Sendable checks.
  • Using callbacks (completion: (Result<...>) -> Void) in new code. That is the pre-async style (old codebases).

notes.title: Unidirectional data flow and The Composable Architecture
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android this is MVI (Orbit, MVIKotlin, Redux-style): a single State, an Intent/Action stream, and a reducer that returns new state plus effects. In iOS the leading framework is The Composable Architecture (TCA) by Point-Free. Redux-like ReSwift is older and less used.

The loop.

 View --send(Action)--> Store --> Reducer(state, action) --> new State --> View re-renders
                                      |
                                      +--> Effect (async work) --> Action (result) --> Reducer

A TCA feature (current style, verify exact API against the version you use).

import ComposableArchitecture

@Reducer
struct CounterFeature {
    @ObservableState
    struct State: Equatable {
        var count = 0
        var fact: String?
        var isLoading = false
    }

    enum Action {
        case incrementTapped
        case factButtonTapped
        case factResponse(String)
    }

    @Dependency(\.factClient) var factClient

    var body: some ReducerOf<Self> {
        Reduce { state, action in
            switch action {
            case .incrementTapped:
                state.count += 1
                return .none
            case .factButtonTapped:
                state.isLoading = true
                return .run { [count = state.count] send in
                    await send(.factResponse(try await factClient.fetch(count)))
                }
            case .factResponse(let fact):
                state.isLoading = false
                state.fact = fact
                return .none
            }
        }
    }
}

struct CounterView: View {
    let store: StoreOf<CounterFeature>

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            Text("\(store.count)")
            Button("+") { store.send(.incrementTapped) }
        }
    }
}

Concepts to know.

  • State is a value type; Action is an enum of everything that can happen (user events and effect results); Reducer is a pure function except for returned Effects; Store runs the loop.
  • Composition: child reducers are scoped into parents with Scope and ifLet/forEach, and navigation is modelled as optional or stack state (@Presents, StackState).
  • Dependencies come from the @Dependency system (swift-dependencies), so tests override them.
  • Testing: TestStore asserts every state change and every received action. Exhaustive testing catches missed effects.
  • Costs: a learning curve, macro-heavy build times, large dependency (swift-syntax compile cost, verify current state), and a framework you must keep updating across major versions.

Comparison with Android MVI.

Concern Android MVI (Orbit etc.) TCA
State holder ViewModel + StateFlow Store
Events sealed Intent Action enum
Side effects viewModelScope.launch / side-effect channel Effect returned from reducer
DI Hilt @Dependency
Navigation as state Nav3 back stack (verify) StackState, @Presents

When to use it. Teams that want exhaustive tests and predictable state, and accept the framework lock-in. Avoid it for small teams that do not already know it, or when you must keep compile times low. Some companies use it for core flows only.

Lightweight alternative. You can get 80 percent of unidirectional flow with a plain @Observable model that exposes func send(_ action: Action) and a private reduce function. No dependency, easy to read.

Real examples. Point-Free's own isowords game, and several fintech and productivity apps publicly use TCA. Meta and Uber use their own internal unidirectional or component frameworks (Uber's RIBs, Meta's ComponentKit and internal Swift frameworks), not TCA.

Analogy. A bank ledger: you never edit the balance directly, you only append a transaction, and the new balance is derived.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing TCA as "Redux for iOS" and stopping there. Mention effects, dependencies, scoping and TestStore.
  • Putting side effects inside the reducer body instead of returning an Effect.
  • Forgetting that large State structs copied on every action need copy-on-write sanity (store big collections as IdentifiedArray or similar).

notes.title: MVC, VIPER and Clean in legacy codebases
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you may have met "God Activities" or MVP with presenters before ViewModel arrived. iOS has the same history: Apple's MVC, then MVP/MVVM, then VIPER and Clean for large teams.

Apple-style MVC (UIKit). The UIViewController is the C, but it also owns the view lifecycle, so it tends to absorb networking, formatting and navigation. This is the origin of the joke "Massive View Controller". Typical old code:

final class ProfileViewController: UIViewController {
    private let nameLabel = UILabel()
    private var user: User?

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        APIClient.shared.fetchUser { [weak self] result in      // completion handler style
            DispatchQueue.main.async {
                if case .success(let user) = result { self?.render(user) }
            }
        }
    }
    private func render(_ user: User) { nameLabel.text = user.name }
}

VIPER. View, Interactor, Presenter, Entity, Router: five types per screen, with protocols between each. Great separation, heavy boilerplate (about 5 files for one screen), and Xcode templates were used to generate them. Common in banks and large enterprises circa 2015 to 2020.

View <-> Presenter <-> Interactor <-> Entity / Services
              |
           Router (creates next module)

Clean Architecture on iOS. Domain layer (entities, use cases, repository protocols) has no UIKit or SwiftUI import; data layer implements the protocols; presentation layer holds view models and views. The dependency rule points inward. Popular example: the "iOS Clean Architecture MVVM" sample projects. It matches the Android Clean Architecture setup you already know.

RIBs (Uber). Router, Interactor, Builder: a tree of business-logic units not tied to views, so logic can be attached and detached independently of screens. Designed for Uber's scale, usually considered overkill otherwise.

Reading a legacy codebase (a practical checklist).

  1. Find the app entry (AppDelegate, SceneDelegate) and how the first screen is built.
  2. Identify the pattern per module; large apps are usually a mix.
  3. Find networking and persistence wrappers (Alamofire, Core Data stack, Realm).
  4. Look for singletons (.shared) that hide dependencies.
  5. Check Combine vs completion handler vs async/await usage per layer.
  6. Do not rewrite. Wrap new SwiftUI features in UIHostingController and migrate incrementally.

Incident patterns. Retain cycles between view controller and presenter (use weak delegate), main-thread work in viewDidLoad blocking launch, and singletons holding stale user state after logout.

Real examples. Many European and Indian banking apps use VIPER; Uber uses RIBs; Lyft and Airbnb described moving away from heavy view controllers toward view models and lightweight components.

Analogy. VIPER is a formal government office with a desk for every form; MVVM is a small shop where two people handle everything.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing MVC as "bad". Apple's MVC is fine when view controllers are kept small via child controllers and separate models.
  • Rewriting everything to SwiftUI at once. Incremental migration is the senior answer.
  • Confusing VIPER's Router with a SwiftUI router: the former builds modules, the latter holds navigation state.

notes.title: Feature modularization with SPM
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you split into Gradle modules (:feature:search, :core:network, :core:ui) with api / implementation dependencies, mostly to speed builds and enforce boundaries. In iOS the tool is Swift Package Manager: local packages inside the repo with several targets each, referenced by the app target.

Typical layout.

MyApp/
  MyApp.xcodeproj
  App/                       (app target: @main, DI wiring, root scene)
  Packages/
    Core/                    (Networking, Persistence, Utilities)
    DesignSystem/            (colors, fonts, reusable views)
    FeatureSearch/           (view, view model, tests)
    FeatureCheckout/
    Domain/                  (models, repository protocols)

A local package manifest:

// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "FeatureSearch",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "FeatureSearch", targets: ["FeatureSearch"])
    ],
    dependencies: [
        .package(path: "../Domain"),
        .package(path: "../DesignSystem")
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "FeatureSearch", dependencies: ["Domain", "DesignSystem"]),
        .testTarget(name: "FeatureSearchTests", dependencies: ["FeatureSearch"])
    ]
)

Access control is the enforcement tool. Types are internal by default, so they are invisible outside the module. Expose only an entry point as public: a view or a factory. package access (Swift 5.9+) lets sibling targets in the same package share symbols without making them public.

public struct SearchFeatureView: View {
    public init(repository: any ProductRepository) { /* ... */ }
    public var body: some View { /* ... */ }
}

Rules that scale.

  • Features depend on Domain and DesignSystem, never on each other. Cross-feature navigation goes through closures or a shared route type defined in a small Navigation module.
  • The app target is the composition root: it creates concrete repositories and injects them.
  • Keep resources (assets, string catalogs) per package using resources: [.process("Resources")] and Bundle.module.
  • Add #Preview per feature so each can be developed without launching the app.
  • Previews and SwiftUI macros inside packages can be slower; measure before splitting every folder.

Alternatives. Tuist or XcodeGen generate Xcode projects from a manifest and are used by many large teams to avoid .pbxproj merge conflicts (Tuist is used at companies like Bumble, verify). Static vs dynamic linking affects launch time: many dynamic frameworks slow pre-main work, so prefer static libraries where possible, or merge dynamically (verify current Xcode options).

Costs. Too many tiny packages increase build graph overhead and complicate previews. Start with 3 to 6 modules (core, design system, domain, a few features) and split further only when build times or ownership demand it.

Real examples. Airbnb, Spotify and Lyft have described modularisation to speed incremental builds; Point-Free open-sources fully modular SPM projects (isowords) as a reference.

Analogy. Shipping containers: each team packs its own, and the port (app target) loads them without opening them.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving everything public which defeats the purpose.
  • Circular dependencies between feature packages (SPM refuses them).
  • Assuming Gradle's implementation vs api has a direct SPM equivalent. Transitive visibility is different; check the target dependency graph.

notes.title: Choosing an architecture for team size and testability
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you would weigh "plain MVVM + Hilt" against "MVI + multi-module". The same trade-off applies: more structure buys testability and parallel work, and costs boilerplate and onboarding time.

Situation Reasonable choice
Solo or 2 devs, MVP SwiftUI + @Observable view models, one app target
3 to 8 devs, growing product MVVM, repository protocols, a few SPM packages
10+ devs, many features Modular SPM, strict boundaries, router, maybe TCA
Legacy UIKit app Keep structure, new screens in SwiftUI inside UIHostingController
Heavy business rules, regulated Clean layers with a framework-free domain package

Decision questions to ask in an interview.

  1. How many engineers will touch this code in a year?
  2. What must be unit tested without a simulator?
  3. Is build time already a pain?
  4. What is the minimum iOS version? (@Observable and SwiftData need iOS 17; below that you need ObservableObject.)
  5. Does the team already know TCA or Combine?

Testability checklist.

  • Every external effect (network, clock, UUID, date, keychain, user defaults) is behind a protocol or a closure.
  • View models are @MainActor classes with injected dependencies and an async entry point to await in tests.
  • Time-based logic uses an injected clock (any Clock<Duration>, or swift-clocks) rather than Task.sleep in tests.
  • UI is verified through snapshot tests (swift-snapshot-testing is a popular library, verify) or XCUITest for a few critical flows.
import Testing

@MainActor
struct CheckoutTests {
    @Test("shows error when payment fails")
    func paymentFailure() async {
        let vm = CheckoutViewModel(payments: FailingPayments(), clock: ImmediateClock())
        await vm.pay()
        #expect(vm.state == .failed("Card declined"))
    }
}

Anti-patterns to name.

  • A "Manager" or "Helper" singleton for everything.
  • View models that import SwiftUI and know about Color or Image.
  • Business logic inside body or in a View extension.
  • Premature modularisation that doubles the number of files with no build time gain.
  • Over-abstracting with generics-heavy protocols (associated types leaking into every signature).

Migration path example. Start: MVVM with @Observable. When two features share logic, extract a use case. When builds slow down, move shared code into a package. If state bugs multiply across screens, evaluate TCA for the complex flows only. Never adopt everything on day one.

Real examples. WWDC sessions "Discover Observation in SwiftUI" and "Data Essentials in SwiftUI" steer toward simple model types. Large employers expect interview answers to mention seams, not frameworks.

Analogy. Choosing between a bicycle, a car and a train: pick by how many people you must move and how far.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering with a pattern name instead of explaining trade-offs against a concrete team size.
  • Ignoring the minimum deployment target when recommending @Observable or SwiftData.
  • Claiming 100 percent unit test coverage is the goal rather than testing seams that carry risk.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• iOS has no single official architecture. Choose by team size, testability and minimum iOS version, and defend the trade-offs.
  • An iOS view model is a plain @Observable @MainActor class owned by the view through @State; there is no ViewModelStore, no onCleared, and no rotation survival. Cancel work via .task and structured concurrency.
  • Model screen state as an enum (idle, loading, content, failed) so illegal states cannot exist; keep stale content during refresh.
  • Repositories are protocols with async throws methods, Sendable implementations and actors for caches; map DTOs to domain models at the boundary; add use cases only for shared or non-trivial logic.
  • TCA is Redux/MVI for Swift: State, Action, Reducer, Effect, Store, @Dependency, TestStore. It buys predictability and costs a learning curve and a dependency.
  • Legacy codebases mix MVC, VIPER, Clean and RIBs; read before rewriting, and migrate incrementally with UIHostingController.
  • Modularise with local SPM packages, expose minimal public API, let the app target be the composition root, and never let features depend on each other.
  • For tests, put every side effect behind a protocol and use Swift Testing with injected fakes and clocks.
